<margin>Su Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039 to 1112, a prominent Song Dynasty scholar</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge. If one day you know the Way, you will look back on worldly deceptions and realize that all is false. By removing the false and returning to your true nature, this is what is called "decreasing." Confucius asked his disciple Zigong: Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all? Zigong replied: Yes, is it not so? Confucius said: No, I permeate everything with a single principle. To forget the worldly mind and restore one's nature is called decreasing. As long as delusions remain, one must continue this process until even the act of forgetting is forgotten. When the mind is pure and nature is restored without remainder, one removes "doing" and reaches the state of "non-doing" <note>original: <term>wu wei</term></note>. People all have the desire to take hold of the world and manage its affairs. Because they create complications and seek external results, their intentions are visible, and things resist them; thus, they encounter difficulty and fail. The Sage practices non-doing, so his mind has no worldly affairs. His inner state is visible externally, and things are at peace with him. Though he does not strive to take the world or manage its affairs, the world and its affairs naturally follow and find peace.

<margin>Lü Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111, a key political figure and philosopher</note></margin>To pursue learning is the path for those who have not yet heard the Way. Because they seek it without knowing it, they must be broad in their study; thus it is said to "increase." To pursue the Way is for those who have already heard it. Because they act upon what they know, they must practice non-doing; thus it is said to "decrease." To "decrease and further decrease" refers to those who have not yet escaped purposeful action. One must decrease even the act of decreasing itself to finally reach the state of non-doing. Non-doing means remaining silent and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one resonates and connects with all circumstances under heaven. To reach non-doing through the act of non-doing is the constant path. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who can attain such supreme divinity? From this we see that to take the world, one must always use non-doing. If one relies on purposeful action, it is clear that such a person is not fit to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai Commentary <note>Huang Maocai, a Southern Song Dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only after one reaches a state of knowing everything can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires a daily increase. Only after one reaches a state of doing nothing can one speak of the Way; therefore, the Way desires a daily decrease. However, "increase" can be pursued through progress, while "decrease" is often difficult to achieve through forced effort. Only those with supreme clarity can suddenly cast off worldly attachments and reach the realm of non-doing. Thus, they can leave nothing undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, spreading through the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai Commentary <note>Li Daochun, a 13th century Taoist master whose literary name was Xizhai</note></margin>The purpose of learning is to seek knowledge, hence the daily increase. The purpose of the Way is to remove delusion, hence the daily decrease. If knowledge is not perfected, the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, one reaches non-doing. Upon reaching non-doing, any purposeful action is itself non-doing. This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of mere increase or decrease. When non-doing reaches its peak, though the world is vast, it is unified by a single principle. If one uses busy-ness to create more business, life becomes difficult and lacks leisure. If even a single object can cause entanglement and error, how much more so the vastness of the world?

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note> of his own; he takes the heart of the people as his heart. To those who are good, I am good. To those who are not good, I am also good. Thus, virtue is goodness. To those who are trustful, I give my trust. To those who are not trustful, I also give my trust. Thus, virtue is trust. <summary>This page contains commentaries on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching, focusing on the distinction between worldly learning (increase) and the pursuit of the Way (decrease). The text explains how reaching a state of non-doing allows a ruler or Sage to harmonize with the world and the hearts of the people.</summary>
<keywords>Tao Te Ching, Laozi, non-doing, wu wei, decrease, increase, Sage, virtue, Su Zhe, Lü Huiqing, Huang Maocai, Li Daochun</keywords>
